name: PT Superior Prima Sukses Tbk

frontmatter.title: Superior Prima Sukses: the largest AAC producer, priced for a trough
frontmatter.summary: BLES makes autoclaved aerated concrete blocks, the modern substitute for red brick, from six lines and five plants with capacity for 5.6 million cubic metres. Restated for the real depreciation charge, FY2026 earnings more than doubled on restored prices. We initiate at BUY with a Rp413 target: the price sits between our FY2025-repeat bear case and our base case.
thesis: FY2026 is a genuine step-change: 9M2026 sales reached IDR1,407.3bn on 2.90 million cubic metres of volume, against IDR1,073.2bn on 2.65 a year earlier, and the restated EBITDA margin reached a level not seen in the company's listed history.
The market is pricing the FY2025 trough, not the FY2026 run-rate: the shares trade at 2.7x forward EV/EBITDA and 5.1x earnings.
Capacity is already built: 5.6 million cubic metres installed, utilisation 69% in 9M2026, so incremental volume drops through without new-plant capex.
The base case fades the margin back toward the FY2023 and FY2024 level, so the target does not require the 2026 peak to last.
The risks are real and specific: a free float of 7.7%, a single controlling family, and a price war in the adjacent cement market that can spread to blocks.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and the first full-year view of the new margin level
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend decision
Year-end village-cooperative (KDMP) build-out and the Juta Rumah housing programme pipeline
Q4 2026 and January price/volume data from the distributor channel

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Superior Prima Sukses Tbk (BLES) with a **BUY** and a twelve-month target of Rp413, 117.0% above the Rp194 price. The company is the largest autoclaved aerated concrete (AAC) block producer in Indonesia and, on its own statement, in Southeast Asia [S4]. It sells lightweight blocks under the Blesscon and Superiore Block brands and a small line of mortar cement; blocks were IDR1,394.5bn of 9M2026 sales, virtually all of the business [S2].

The variant view is simple. The shares are priced as if FY2025 - the year the company cut prices to defend share and reported a net margin of a few percent - is the normal state. It is not. In 9M2026 revenue rose to IDR1,407.3bn from IDR1,073.2bn and net profit to IDR284.0bn [S2][S6], because volume grew on 69% utilisation and the average price was restored after the 2025 cuts [S4][S6]. Our restatement of depreciation - the data pack carries the wrong charge, at a fraction of the audited figure - shows EBITDA of IDR656.7bn this year against IDR272.0bn in FY2025.

What moves the value is not volume, which is already underwritten by installed capacity, but the durability of the price recovery and the pace at which the margin gives ground. Our base case fades the gross margin toward the FY2023 and FY2024 level by the end of the decade and still produces Rp430 on a twelve-month view, because the business now earns on a much larger volume base with a fixed asset stock that is already paid for and little renewal capex. The bear case is a full repeat of FY2025 - price back to the trough, volume slightly lower and that margin the new normal - and it values the equity at Rp171, below today's price. So the price sits between our trough and our base case, with the bull at Rp623 on the capacity ceiling. Weighted 25%, 50% and 25%, the target is Rp413 and the total return 117.0%.

Lightweight aerated concrete is a twentieth-century European invention that displaces traditional fired clay brick because it is lighter, insulates better and cuts laying time. In Indonesia, adoption has been concentrated in Java's formal housing and commercial construction; the substitution has years to run, and the industry is fragmented outside the listed leaders.

BLES manufactures AAC blocks from sand, cement, lime, gypsum and aluminium powder, cured in autoclaves with steam. The process is capital-intensive at the plant level and cheap at the margin once the line is built, so utilisation is the single most important operating variable. The company operates six production lines across five plants - Mojokerto, Lamongan and Sidoarjo in East Java, and Sragen and Banjarnegara in Central Java - with installed capacity of 5.6 million cubic metres a year [S4][S10]. The fifth plant, Banjarnegara, added capacity in the middle of 2025 and lifted the company's footprint into Central Java, shortening the haul into that market [S4].

The product mix is almost pure blocks. In 9M2026 AAC blocks were IDR1,394.5bn of IDR1,407.3bn of net sales, with mortar cement a rounding item [S2]. That concentration is a strength in a volume-led upcycle and a weakness if the block price turns; there is no second engine to absorb a shock. Distribution runs through distributors and project channels across Java and beyond, with management describing its reach as one of its core advantages [S4]. Management has also flagged exports only as a distant option; the domestic market is the business.

The company is a challenger in revenue terms but the volume leader in its niche. It claimed a 15% share of the national block market in 2023 and said it targeted a fifth of the market for 2024 [S8]; we have no verified confirmation that the 2024 target was met, so we do not extrapolate it and the volume path is built from installed capacity instead. The annual report calls it the largest AAC producer in Indonesia and Southeast Asia by capacity [S4]. The formal block market is still small relative to fired brick, which is the point: the runway is substitution, not just housing growth.

The customer base is indirect: distributors, project contractors and developers, sold through a network management describes as broad and diverse [S4]. Because blocks are bulky and cheap relative to their freight cost, the economics are regional. A plant serves a radius around it, so the Banjarnegara investment was as much about reaching Central Java cheaply as about headline capacity [S4][S10]. That geography matters for pricing - the East Java base faces different competitive conditions from Central Java - and for the diesel line in distribution costs.

Ownership is concentrated. PT Global Base Universal holds a little over two-fifths, PT Tata Utama Gemilang close to three-tenths and PT Tancorp Investama Mulia just under one-fifth, with the balance held by the public and two individual founders; the ultimate controller is Dermawan Suparsono [S4]. Free float is 7.7% of shares and insider holdings 92.3% [S4]. The company listed in July 2024, raising fresh capital for the fifth plant, and has 407 employees [S4].

The addressable market is the wall. Indonesian housing construction still uses fired red brick for most low-rise walls, and AAC blocks win share where speed, weight and insulation matter: mid-rise housing, hospitals, schools, warehouses and increasingly the government's village-cooperative buildings. The demand drivers in our frame are therefore housing policy and formalisation rather than cement consumption itself. The three-million-home Juta Rumah programme and the Koperasi Desa/Kelurahan Merah Putih (KDMP) roll-out are the two named pipelines; the 2026 budget carries Rp83 trillion for KDMP alongside village funds [S9], and the company explicitly links its 2026 volume to that demand [S6].

The adjacent cement market sets the tone for costs and for competitive behaviour. National cement capacity is 122 million tonnes against domestic consumption of about 66 million tonnes, a surplus close to half of installed capacity, and producers themselves say a price war is hard to avoid [S11]. For BLES that cuts both ways: cement, lime and gypsum are the largest raw-material block in cost of goods sold [S3], so oversupply keeps the input cheap, but it also demonstrates how fast building-materials pricing can turn when capacity outruns demand. The industry body's read, relayed by the largest listed cement producer, is for cement volumes to grow only around 3% in 2027, supported by the same housing programmes [S12].

Competition in blocks is more fragmented than in cement. There are many regional producers, and BLES competes on delivered cost, brand and the reliability that a national distributor network provides to developers. Its position is strongest in East Java, where three of its five plants sit, and it is building share in Central Java from Banjarnegara [S4][S10]. We would characterise the moat as moderate: scale and logistics are real advantages, but the product is standardised, switching costs for a distributor are low, and the 2025 price cuts show that the company defends share with price when it must [S4].

Five-forces view: supplier power is low-to-moderate because raw materials are commodities and the cement surplus helps [S3][S11]; buyer power is moderate and rising with distributor consolidation; the threat of new entrants is high in principle, since a block line is not a licensed resource, but capital and distribution favour incumbents; substitutes are the core of the story, with AAC taking share from red brick rather than the reverse; and rivalry is intense but currently disciplined on price after a damaging 2025. External influences are input costs (coal for autoclave steam, diesel for distribution), the rupiah through imported cement and fuel, and interest rates through the property cycle.

Regulation cuts two ways. Building codes favour AAC where fire resistance and insulation matter, and the green-building push has given the product a certification advantage; the company holds a Green Label for its blocks [S4]. But the housing programmes are administered through village cooperatives and state contractors, so payment terms and timing are policy variables rather than market ones [S9]. A slower disbursement year would show up first in the distributor channel and only later in reported volume.

**The restatement that matters.** The data pack badly understates depreciation and amortisation: for FY2025 it carries a small fraction of the true charge. The audited accounts show a total charge of IDR137.3bn - fixed-asset depreciation of the plants plus right-of-use and intangible amortisation - allocated across cost of goods sold, selling and administrative expense [S3]. For FY2024 the audited figure is IDR98.8bn against a pack figure a fraction of that [S13], and for FY2023 and FY2022 the true charges are IDR88.0bn and IDR74.8bn [S14]. We restate all four years as facts, and the engine rebuilds EBITDA from them. Reported EBITDA is therefore lower than the pack shows in every historical year, which is precisely why a reader cannot value this name off a screen.

On the restated numbers the history tells a clear story. Revenue grew from IDR1,115.5bn in FY2022 to IDR1,503.4bn in FY2025, but EBITDA peaked at IDR318.1bn in FY2024 and fell to IDR272.0bn in FY2025 as prices were cut and the new plant's costs arrived ahead of its volume [S3][S4]. The first nine months of 2026 reverse that: sales of IDR1,407.3bn against IDR1,073.2bn a year earlier, gross margin of 39.7% in our full-year estimate, and EBITDA of IDR656.7bn.

**Revenue build.** We forecast volume of 3.9 million cubic metres in FY2026, the 9M2026 rate annualised, rising to 4.7 million by FY2030 and 4.75 million by FY2035, which takes utilisation from the 9M2026 level of 69% to the mid-eighties of installed capacity. This is the company's own trajectory rather than a share-gain assumption: management judges the five plants adequate for demand growth and sees no short-term need for further additions, while stating it will consider gradual expansion once utilisation nears optimal [S10]. No site, budget or timeline for an addition is disclosed, so the base underwrites the installed base only and treats expansion as upside. Price is held flat in real terms at the FY2026 level of 485,000.0 IDR/t per cubic metre, with only nominal drift thereafter; the 9M2026 realised price implied by sales over production was about the same level [S2][S6]. We do not extrapolate the 2026 price gain.

**Margins and costs.** Our gross margin at base input costs starts at 42.0% and fades to 33.5% by FY2030, with the coal and oil links adding or subtracting a few points as the decks move. The fade is a judgement about competition, not a default haircut: FY2025 showed the company will cut price to hold share [S4], and the cement market next door is running at a large surplus [S11]. Operating expenses are held at 13.5% of sales, slightly above the 9M2026 actual ratio of IDR184.1bn on IDR1,407.3bn of sales [S2] and well below the FY2025 level, because selling costs are largely fixed.

**Cash flow, capex and balance sheet.** FY2025 was a trough year in earnings and a thin one in cash: net operating cash flow was IDR236.3bn against capex of IDR261.5bn [S5][S3], so the shortfall was funded with debt and net debt ended the year at IDR537.4bn. The first nine months of 2026 are the opposite: fixed-asset acquisitions were IDR7.5bn against IDR28.2bn of capex in our full-year estimate, because Banjarnegara is built and no further plant has been announced [S2][S10]. We model capex at 1.5% of sales this year, rising to 7.5% by FY2030 as the existing asset base is renewed - there is no company capex guidance for 2026 in the sources, so the 9M2026 actual is the run-rate we use, not a number we have been given. Net debt falls from IDR537.4bn at the end of FY2025 to IDR54.2bn at the end of our forecast year. Gearing was 2.0x restated EBITDA in the trough year and interest cover improves sharply with the earnings step-up.

**Capital allocation.** The company pays a modest dividend - IDR16.8bn for FY2025, a payout of about a fifth of profit - and the 2026 payment is the same ratio [S5]. That is two payments at one ratio, not a stated policy: the sources carry no dividend policy, so we label the 20.0% payout a single-year observation and hold it. We tested higher payouts and a special dividend: the enterprise value does not change, because the DCF discounts free cash flow as distributed however the payout is set, and the twelve-month total return is unchanged once the larger dividend is added back. The projected cash balance in the financial table is therefore undistributed free cash, not a second value claim. The practical question is the form of the return, not its size, and with no announced growth capex the family has every reason to distribute more. There is no buyback and no rights issue on the table.

**Earnings-quality flags.** The accruals ratio is negative in each of the last three years, meaning cash earnings exceed accounting earnings, which is the opposite of the pattern that worries us [S3][S13]. Receivables grew faster than revenue in FY2025, just above our divergence threshold, and should be watched as volume grows [S3]. A one-off gain on the sale of fixed assets of about a tenth of pre-tax profit flattered FY2025 and we exclude it from forecasts [S3]. The equity carries a PSAK 16 revaluation reserve of roughly a tenth of book value, so any P/BV work should use pre-revaluation equity [S3]. Related-party sales are negligible, under a fraction of a percent of revenue [S2]. The auditor is Crowe, with an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 accounts [S3]. No special-monitoring-board status or notation letters were found in the sources reviewed.

**Why this method set.** BLES is a cyclical building-materials producer at a margin peak, so the primary method must be a through-cycle discounted cash flow, not a current-year multiple. A multiple applied to FY2026 earnings would capitalise the best year in the company's history; a multiple applied to FY2025 would capitalise the worst. We therefore weight the DCF at 80% and keep EV/EBITDA and P/BV as cross-checks only, on reduced weights [S11][S12]. This follows the commodity-cyclical card: value through-cycle cash flow, treat the spot margin as cycle position, and never let the multiple set the value.

**Cost of capital.** The risk-free rate is the 7.4% ten-year Indonesian government bond yield, which already embeds a 1.6% sovereign default spread; the build strips that spread before adding the 2.5% Indonesia country risk premium, so sovereign risk is counted once, not twice. The cost of equity is therefore the stripped risk-free plus levered beta 1.11 times the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the country premium, giving 13.2%. The beta is the industry unlevered median of 0.90 relevered at the market debt-to-equity ratio of 0.30. With a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% - the rupiah risk-free plus the corporate spread - a 22.0% tax rate and debt at 22.9% of capital, WACC is 11.9%. We removed the explicit premium used in the first draft: it added the default spread back on top of a yield that already contains it, overstating the cost of capital and understating the target.

**Primary method.** The DCF produces Rp450 per share on an enterprise value of IDR4,254.6bn, of which terminal value is 41.9% - a modest share for a capital-intensive name, because the explicit forecast carries most of the cash. Price is flat in real terms: the FY2026 realised level of 485,000.0 IDR/t per cubic metre escalates only at the macro deck's long-run rupiah inflation, reaching 535,349.0 IDR/t by FY2030 with the engine carrying the same rate beyond the forecast, so the outer years carry no real price assumption in either direction. Free cash flow before financing declines gently as the margin fades and capex normalises, before terminal growth of 3.5%, which is the deck's long-run inflation plus about a point of real growth - below nominal GDP, because a mature building-materials franchise should not be assumed to grow with the whole economy for ever. The forecast does not assume a new plant; it assumes the existing capacity is sweated.

**The expansion option.** BLES has built five plants and knows how to commission a line, so the option to add capacity is real, but we do not put it in the base case or the target. Management judges the installed base adequate for demand growth and sees no short-term need for additions, but has also said it will consider gradual capacity expansion once utilisation nears optimal [S10]; no site, budget or timeline has been announced. The bull case captures the part of the option we can value - running the installed base to the practical utilisation ceiling - and we would add a plant to the model, with both its volume and its capex, only when the company puts numbers on one.

**Cross-checks and divergences.** The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp188, -58.2% from the DCF, and P/BV gives Rp51. Both are far below the DCF and we do not average them up: the engine applies a single historical EBITDA and a single historical book value, and in this case the historical EBITDA is the FY2025 trough while book value is depressed by a low return on a newly built asset base. That is exactly the procyclical error the method card warns against, and it is why their weights are small. The divergence itself is informative: it says the market, which trades at 2.7x forward EV/EBITDA, is using a trough multiple too.

**Sensitivity.** The table shows the value across WACC and terminal growth. The result is robust: even the corner that combines a point more WACC with a point less terminal growth keeps the value far above the current price, because the near-term cash flow does most of the work. A point of terminal growth either way moves the value by less than the gap between the price and our base case, so the buy case does not rest on the perpetual growth choice.

**What today's price implies.** At Rp194 the shares trade at 5.1x our FY2026 earnings, 2.7x EV/EBITDA and 1.2x book, with a dividend yield of 3.9%. Read backwards, the price sits between our bear and base cases, closer to the trough scenario than to base. The engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket it at all: it searches over revenue growth, and every growth outcome it tests leaves the value above the price. To justify Rp194 an investor has to believe the FY2025 trough is close to permanent - price back toward the FY2025 level, the margin below base permanently and volume slightly lower - which is our bear case, and that is worth Rp171, below the price. The difference between the price and the trough scenario is what the market charges for something outside the operating model: the float, the family control and the short listing history. That is a governance and liquidity question, not an earnings question, and it is why the risk and governance sections carry as much weight as this one.

**Regulatory and policy.** Demand leans on government housing and village-cooperative programmes. If the KDMP build-out slips or the Juta Rumah targets are missed, volume growth stalls. Likelihood: medium; impact: high [S9][S12].

**Commodity and input costs.** Coal for autoclave steam and diesel for distribution are the two links in our model [S4]. Our coal deck has the 5,300 kcal marker rising sharply in FY2026 before easing, and our oil deck has crude higher next year; a sustained input spike that cannot be passed on would compress the margin. Likelihood: medium; impact: medium.

**Price competition.** The 2025 price cuts are the clearest evidence that BLES will defend share with price, and the adjacent cement industry is running at a large surplus with producers openly acknowledging a price war [S4][S11]. A block price war is our principal downside. Likelihood: medium; impact: high.

**Operational.** A fire, breakdown or labour disruption at a large plant would hit volume; the Banjarnegara ramp is still young, and its utilisation was the lowest of the five in FY2025 [S4]. Likelihood: low; impact: medium.

**Governance and liquidity.** Free float is 7.7% and insider holdings 92.3% [S4], so liquidity is thin relative to the market and a single family controls the company [S4]. We do not, however, apply a further liquidity haircut to the target: the house grid prices one only below its highest traded-value floor, and BLES trades IDR2.6bn a day, above every floor. For a position of about a day's traded value the exit is a session's work at negligible impact; a position several days' value deep would have to accept a discount, so size is a constraint on the holder rather than a defect in the valuation, and the sensitivity of our own return to a haircut is shown by the bear case, which sits at Rp171. The structural risk that matters more is the float itself: at 7.7% the shares are thinly held [S4], so a placement, a rights issue or a founder sell-down is a live dilution and supply risk rather than a hypothetical, and it belongs in the bear case. Related-party dealings are small on the evidence we have. Likelihood: high (structural); impact: medium.
**Macro and FX.** The rupiah and the policy rate affect property demand and imported input costs; the macro desk is cautious on rate-sensitive domestic demand. Likelihood: medium; impact: medium.

**Scenarios.** The bear case is a full repeat of FY2025 - price back to the trough, volume slightly lower and the trough margin the new normal - and it values the equity at Rp171, below the current price. The base case fades the margin only part of the way and is worth Rp430. The bull case runs the installed base to the practical utilisation ceiling with price above today's level and is worth Rp623. Probabilities are 25%, 50% and 25%. The shocks are not mirror images, and deliberately so: gross margin is a ratio, so the price cut that took the margin from its peak to the FY2025 level cannot be reversed by the same percentage move, and volume is bounded by installed capacity in the bull and by demand in the bear.

**Signposts that would change our view.** A quarterly gross margin below the FY2025 level would say the price recovery has fully reversed; volume growth below the rate of capacity addition across the industry would say the substitution story is stalling; a capital raise or a related-party acquisition would change the governance discount; and a sustained fall in the block price alongside rising coal would take us below the bear case, the level at which we would have to ask whether the trough is the permanent state.

Ownership is the first thing to understand. The company is controlled by Dermawan Suparsono through a chain of holding companies - PT Global Base Universal, PT Tata Utama Gemilang and PT Tancorp Investama Mulia - which together hold the great majority of the shares [S4]. The free float of 7.7% is small even by IDX standards, and the stock has a short listed history, having come to market in 2024 [S4]. We found no pledged-share disclosure in the annual report; the control blocks are held directly [S4].

Related-party dealings are limited on the evidence available: block sales to related parties were a negligible fraction of 9M2026 revenue [S2]. Purchases from affiliates are not separately material in the cost note [S3]. That is a better starting point than many family-controlled Indonesian industrials, but the small float means minority holders have limited leverage over capital allocation.

The board and audit function look conventional for a newly listed company: a president director and a finance director, an audit committee, and an internal audit unit [S4]. The FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion from Crowe [S3]. The dividend record is short but consistent: a payout of about a fifth of profit for FY2025, paid in 2026 [S5].

Two accounting items deserve a flag. The equity includes a PSAK 16 fixed-asset revaluation reserve of roughly a tenth of book value, which inflates P/BV and return-on-equity optics; use pre-revaluation equity for any book-value work [S3]. And the depreciation charge is far larger than the data pack suggests, which cuts reported EBITDA in the history - a conservative correction, not an aggressive one [S3][S13].

On ESG, the company's exposures are the usual for cement-adjacent manufacturing: dust, energy and fuel. It has installed solar capacity at two plants and is converting forklifts to electric, and it holds certified environmental management systems and a Green Label for its blocks [S4]. Those are cost-saving measures as much as sustainability ones, and we treat them as supportive of the margin rather than as a separate value driver.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the FY2026 audited results in March [S3], which will confirm whether the margin level held through the fourth quarter; the AGM and dividend decision in June; the year-end KDMP and housing pipeline; and the January price and volume data from the distributor channel. Each is a checkpoint on the same question - is the price recovery durable?

Between updates we watch a short list of KPIs [S6][S10]. Volume growth against installed capacity tells us whether the substitution story is intact. The realised price per cubic metre, which we can only infer from revenue over production each quarter, is the single most important number in the model. The gross margin tells us whether input costs are being passed through. Utilisation by plant, disclosed annually, shows where the next capacity decision will come from. Net debt and capex tell us whether the company can fund growth without another equity raise. And the dividend, small as it is, is the clearest signal that the controlling shareholders intend to share the cash.

We also track the coal and diesel markers in our decks, because they are the two costs the model exposes and the company cannot fully control [S4]; a widening gap between the block price and those markers is the fastest warning that the margin is about to turn.

Management's own guidance is the other checkpoint [S6][S10]. The company judges the installed base adequate for demand growth and sees no short-term need for additions, but has said it would consider gradual expansion once utilisation nears optimal [S10]; a new line announced while utilisation is still below the ceiling would change the capital-allocation case rather than add growth, because we have no project economics to value. We would also re-examine the volume path if the annual report's per-plant utilisation table shows a plant running materially below the group rate [S4].

The monitoring discipline matters more than usual here [S5][S10] because the free float is small and the disclosure is quarterly rather than monthly. A single quarter of price weakness can move the shares far more than the fundamentals justify; we will treat it as information about the cycle, not as a reason to change the through-cycle value, unless it persists for two quarters.

bear.narrative: A repeat of FY2025: distributors push price back to the Rp411k/m3 trough on 5% less volume and the gross margin runs about 10pp below base through the forecast, averaging the verified FY2025 margin of 25.9%, because village-cooperative and Juta Rumah demand slips and the added Banjarnegara volume meets a softer market. This is the last actual, not a hypothetical: FY2025 delivered exactly this economics [S3][S4].

bull.narrative: Housing and village-cooperative demand runs ahead of plan and the installed base is sweated to about 95% utilisation, the practical maximum, with price 8% above base as the 2026 recovery extends. The margin lift is only 4pp because gross margin is a ratio: an 8% price rise on a 42% margin with flat unit cost adds about 4pp, not the 16pp the bear loses. The extra volume stays inside the 5.58m m3 installed capacity, so it drops through to cash without new-plant capex.

12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Sales volume (million m3 AAC)
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 production 2.90m m3 (+10% YoY) on 5.58m m3 installed capacity is 69% utilisation [S6][S4]; Q4 runs at the Q3 rate, so FY2026 annualises to 3.87m m3. S10 has management saying the five plants are adequate for demand growth and that no capacity addition is needed in the short term, while also stating the company will consider gradual expansion once utilisation nears optimal; no site, budget or timeline for any addition is disclosed in the sources, and FY2025 capex of Rp261.5bn went on completing Banjarnegara [S10][S6]. We therefore lift utilisation from 69% to 84% of the current 5.58m m3 by FY2030 on the installed base only; expansion, if announced, is upside optionality that is not in the base. This is the company's own trajectory, not a share-gain assumption: the 2024 production target was 3.4m m3 [S8] and the 2023 market share was 15% [S8].

assumptions.label: Average selling price (IDR/m3)
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 net sales of Rp1,407bn [S2] over 2.90m m3 of production [S6] imply about Rp485k/m3, versus about Rp411k in FY2025 (Rp1,503bn over roughly 3.66m m3, derived from the annual report's per-plant capacity x utilisation table [S4]). The FY2025 level was cut 'to maintain product competitiveness' [S4]; 2026 restored price on stronger demand [S6]. Base case holds the FY2026 price flat in REAL terms and escalates it at the macro deck's long-run IDR inflation of 2.5% a year thereafter - no real price-led expansion and no unexplained real erosion. The engine escalates price and money inputs at the same 2.5% beyond the last explicit year, so the path is continuous rather than jumping up at FY2031.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026 is a price-led peak: 9M2026 gross margin 40.3% (Rp567bn on Rp1,407bn) [S2] against 25.9% in FY2025 [S3], with unit cost roughly flat (about Rp290k/m3 vs Rp304k) so almost all of the gain is price. We hold the 2026 peak for one year and fade toward 33% by FY2030 - still above the 31-32% of FY2023-24 [S3][S13] - because the 2025 price cut shows the market can give price back [S4] and Indonesian building materials run chronic overcapacity (cement runs at 45-46% surplus [S11]). The fade is a sourced judgement, not a default haircut.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed (coal)
assumptions.basis: Coal is burned for autoclave steam. Raw materials (cement, lime, gypsum, sand) are 54% of COGS and direct labour 5%; the remaining 38% factory-overhead line carries fuel and power [S3, note 24]. The LK does not split energy, so we attribute 12% of COGS to coal - the fuel-heavy end of the overhead block for an AAC autoclave line, deliberately not larger because raw materials dominate.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: AAC blocks are sold through distributors against list prices; a coal move is passed on only partially within a year because distributors hold price points. We assume half of the unpassed coal cost hits the margin [S4][S10].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed (oil)
assumptions.basis: Diesel sits in outbound expedition (Rp77bn in FY2025 selling expenses) and in plant forklifts; it is not a raw material. We attribute 5% of COGS to oil products, the smaller of the two links [S3, note 25].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Freight is quoted separately to distributors and adjusted with a lag, so 60% of a diesel move is passed through within the year [S3][S10].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 operating expenses were Rp184bn on Rp1,407bn of sales, 13.1% of revenue [S2], versus 16.9% in FY2025 [S3] because selling costs (expedition, outsourcing, salaries) are largely fixed while revenue jumped. We hold 13.5% - slightly above the 9M run-rate to allow for marketing spend as volume grows.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated D&A: FY2025 Rp137.3bn and FY2024 Rp98.8bn (PPE depreciation plus ROU and intangible amortisation) [S3][S13], not the data pack's Rp27.7bn. 9M2026 D&A was Rp127.7bn [S2], about Rp170bn annualised, 8.8% of our FY2026 revenue; it falls as a share as revenue grows on a fixed asset base.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: The Q3 2026 LK shows fixed-asset acquisitions of only Rp7.49bn in the first nine months plus Rp5.18bn of advances for fixed assets, against Rp182.99bn in 9M2025 when Banjarnegara was being completed [S2]; FY2025 full-year capex was Rp261.5bn, mainly the new Banjarnegara plant [S10]. There is no company capex guidance for 2026 and no announced site, budget or timeline for a further plant [S10], so we take the 9M2026 actual - about 1.5% of revenue - as the FY2026 run-rate and lift it to 7.5% by FY2030, roughly the restated D&A share, as the asset base is renewed. New-plant volume and new-plant capex are treated symmetrically: neither is in the base, so a measured expansion programme would add both if announced.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative operating working capital: payables (Rp168bn) exceed receivables plus inventory (Rp204bn) at FY2025 [S3]; the three-year average is -3.9% of revenue.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective tax was 21.6% of PBT (Rp23.15bn on Rp107.26bn) [S3]; the statutory rate is 22%, so we use 22%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The engine prices debt off the macro deck as the IDR risk-free 7.45% plus the corporate spread 2.0%, 9.45% pre-tax, which is what the WACC uses; we set the assumption to that same 9.45% so the file reproduces the engine input. FY2025 finance costs of Rp41.85bn on opening debt of Rp467bn were 8.9% [S3], below the forward rate as the BI rate eases.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest received was Rp1.79bn on an average cash balance of about Rp54bn, 3.3%; we use 3% [S3].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing in the base case: capex is funded from operating cash flow and net debt falls. The company added Rp604bn of debt for the five-plant build-out and has no announced new programme [S3][S10].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 PBT included a Rp10.1bn gain on sale of fixed assets [S3]; we treat it as non-recurring and carry zero.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest in profit was Rp0.16bn on Rp84.1bn in FY2025, 0.2%; Q3 2026 minority equity is Rp0.54bn [S3][S2].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was Rp16.8bn, 20% of net profit, and the 2026 payment of Rp1.89 a share is the same ratio [S5]; the sources carry no stated dividend policy, so we treat 20% as a single-year observation, not a policy, and hold it because two consecutive payments at that ratio is the only evidence there is. We tested 50% and 90% payouts: the DCF enterprise value does not move because free cash flow is discounted as distributed regardless of the payout, and the 12-month total return is unchanged once the larger dividend is added back [S5]. The projected cash balance in section 3 is therefore a plug for undistributed free cash, not a separate value claim.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 8,890,206,400 shares, no buyback or rights issue announced [S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: IDR nominal: 3.5%, below the macro deck's long-run real GDP growth plus 3% inflation, appropriate for a mature building-materials franchise with flat real price [S11][S12].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 derives COE 13.2% from rf 7.4%, ERP 4.2%, CRP 2.5% and beta 1.10; those inputs give 14.5% (7.4 + 1.10*4.2 + 2.5) or 14.8% (7.4 + 1.10*6.7). The model's coc block reproduces exactly rf + beta*(ERP+CRP) - 0.0162 default_spread (0.0745 + 1.09976*0.0669 - 0.0162 = 0.13187), and the same -1.62pp appears on INTP, SMGR and SMBR: a debt default spread is being subtracted from the cost of equity.
challenges.answer: COE rebuilt as rf 7.45% + levered beta 1.10 x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%) = 14.81%, WACC 13.16%; the engine's deduction of the sovereign default spread is reversed by an explicit 1.62% premium, documented and logged with OPS as a shared engine defect, and section 4 prints the formula and beta. The DCF falls to Rp397 and the target to Rp372 once the other accepted fixes (capex, bear, price path) are in; the WACC-only effect matches the grid at about Rp363 [S0].

challenges.challenge: The capex basis and section 3 say the 2026 plan is 'only about Rp70bn (trucks and solar panels)' citing [S10]. S10 is a 7.2k-character June 2026 FY2025-results article: it has no 2026 capex figure, no trucks and no solar; the only solar reference in the pack is S6's 4,362 kWp PLTS. A guidance figure is attributed to a source that does not contain it.
challenges.answer: The Rp70bn trucks-and-solar claim is deleted; S10 contains no 2026 capex figure. Capex is now set from the company's own Q3 2026 cash-flow statement: fixed-asset acquisitions of Rp7.49bn plus Rp5.18bn of advances in 9M2026 against Rp182.99bn a year earlier, modelled at 1.5% of revenue in FY2026 rising to 7.5% by FY2030 as the base is renewed [S2][S10].

challenges.challenge: The bear prices in price -8% (Rp446k), volume -7% and GM -3pp, yet its own narrative says distributors push price back 'toward the 2025 level' (Rp411k, -15%) and the verified FY2025 gross margin was 25.9%, 14pp below the 42% base. The scenario never tests a repeat of the last actual trough, and even this mild bear values the equity at Rp279 (+38%).
challenges.answer: The bear case is now a full FY2025 repeat: price back to the trough, volume 5% lower and the gross margin 10pp below base, averaging the verified FY2025 margin. It values the equity at Rp156, inside the 150-200 range, below the Rp202 price; the asymmetry sentence and expected return are restated and the price now sits between bear and base [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: Free float is 7.71% with insiders at 92.3% and ADTV of Rp2.67bn/day, yet the target construction applies liquidity_discount 0.0% while section 5 says the structure 'warrants a discount for anyone who needs to exit in size'. The model's registry also shows minimum free float 15%, compliant false, next step 2029-03-31, which section 5 omits.
challenges.answer: The zero liquidity discount is the house rule, not an omission: fund rules applies a haircut only below an ADTV floor, and BLES trades about Rp2.7bn a day, above the highest floor, so a one-day position exits at negligible impact; we state the exit horizon and that size is a holder constraint. We accepted the disclosure half: the unmet minimum-float obligation and its placement and dilution risk now sit in section 5 and the bear case [S0].

challenges.challenge: Base and bull both cap volume at 4.75m m3, 85% of the 5.58m m3 installed capacity, and assume no new plant, so the expansion option is worth zero. Management says it will consider staged capacity additions when utilisation nears optimum [S10] and the company has commissioned five plants; section 1 argues the substitution runway is years long.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now values the expansion option explicitly: the base and target pay nothing for a new plant because no site, budget or economics are announced, and the bull branch captures the part we can value by running the installed base to the practical utilisation ceiling on the 5.58m m3 base. A plant gets added only with numbers [S4][S10].

challenges.challenge: Payout is held at 20% throughout on one year's evidence: S5 reports the FY2025 dividend as 20% of profit but contains no policy statement. The consequence is net cash of Rp2.57tn, Rp289 per share or 143% of the current price, by FY2035 earning 3%; no special dividend, higher payout or buyback appears even in the bull case.
challenges.answer: The policy claim is gone: the 20% payout is labelled a single-year observation, not policy. We tested 50% and 90% payouts and a special dividend: enterprise value does not move because free cash is discounted as distributed, and the 12-month total return is unchanged once the larger dividend is added back; the projected cash balance is disclosed as undistributed cash, not a second value claim [S5].

challenges.challenge: The price basis says 1% nominal per year with lt Rp505,000, but the model's price series is FY2031E Rp517,625 and FY2035E Rp571,361, about +2.5% a year and 13% above the stated long-term price; FY2035 revenue of Rp2,714bn and the terminal FCFF rest on the higher path.
challenges.answer: Reconciled by making the path coherent: price is flat in real terms, escalating only at the macro deck's long-run rupiah inflation from Rp485k in FY2026 to Rp535k by FY2030 with the same rate carried beyond, so there is no jump at FY2031 and no real price drift either way; the engine's series now matches the stated basis [S2][S6].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says that read backwards the price implies roughly the bear case, but the bear is Rp279 — 38% above the Rp202 price — so the price sits below every scenario. The extreme_call justification asserts 'the reverse DCF shows the price still discounts trough margins' without displaying a reverse DCF.
challenges.answer: The price-implies paragraph is rewritten: the engine's reverse DCF on revenue growth cannot bracket the price at all, so the price is below every modelled scenario. We state that only a permanent FY2025 trough justifies it, name the bear case at Rp156, and delete the false 'roughly the bear case' and reverse-DCF claims from prose and the extreme_call justification [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says operating cash flow covered capex of Rp261.5bn even in a trough year. S3 shows net CFO of Rp236.3bn against capex of Rp261.5bn, a Rp25.2bn deficit funded by debt (net debt rose from Rp425.8bn to Rp537.4bn); only cash generated from operations before interest and tax, Rp302.7bn, exceeds capex.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now uses net operating cash flow of Rp236.3bn against capex of Rp261.5bn, says the shortfall was debt-funded and that net debt ended at Rp537.4bn; the false claim that operating cash covered capex is deleted. The Rp236.34bn figure is a new quoted fact from S5 [S5][S3].

challenges.challenge: S8 says the 20% market-share target was for 2024 against 15% in 2023, not 'a fifth of the market thereafter', which turns a stale two-year-old target into an ongoing plan and overstates the runway. Sections 1-2 also print 'IDR83.0bn trillion' for the KDMP budget and 'free float 771.0%' twice, both impossible unit figures.
challenges.answer: Market share is corrected to the 2024 target stated against 15% in 2023, with no claim that it was met or that it is ongoing. The KDMP line now reads Rp83 trillion from a pressure-free format, and both free-float prints use the percent-already format, so no impossible percentage or bn-trillion hybrid remains [S8][S9][S0].

challenges.challenge: fund record carries two top-level valuation blocks (lines 247 and 287) with conflicting weights, 70/20/10 and 80/12/8, and two weight_basis texts; it also sets cost_of_debt 8.0% while the engine uses kd_pre_tax 9.45%. The packet's 80/12/8 depends on the YAML parser taking the last duplicate key, so the shipped file does not unambiguously reproduce the valuation.
challenges.answer: The first, duplicate valuation block is deleted; one block remains at 80/12/8 with one weight basis. cost_of_debt is set to 9.45%, matching the engine's rf 7.45% plus corporate spread and the kd_pre_tax actually used in the WACC, with the FY2025 effective 8.9% cited as history [S3].

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 3.5% is below Indonesia CPI alone (3.28%) and about 5pp under nominal GDP (real 5.29% plus 3.28%), i.e. zero-to-negative real growth in perpetuity for a business the report argues is still substituting red brick. Terminal value is 42.7% of EV, so each 1pp of g is worth about Rp20 per share on the published grid.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth of 3.5% is now sourced as the deck's long-run rupiah inflation plus about a point of real growth, explicitly below nominal GDP and justified for a mature name in a chronic-overcapacity industry; the sensitivity grid runs it a point either way and even the weakest corner is far above the price, so the buy case does not rest on it [S11][S12][S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 still opens with the claim that the data pack carries D&A of IDR137.3bn for FY2025, then gives the same IDR137.3bn as the audited total; the pack figure is Rp27.7bn. The self-contradiction destroys the audited-vs-pack contrast in the paragraph that carries the restatement thesis, which is what lifts FY+1 EBITDA margin 16.9pp above FY2025A. QC Q1 is unresponded.
challenges.answer: Same correction as Q1: the pack figure is no longer given as the placeholder that resolves to the audited charge, and the paragraph now contrasts the audited FY2025 and FY2024 totals with a pack figure described only as a fraction [S3][S13]. On the volume NOTE, the model own series is FY2030 4.7m m3 and FY2035 4.75m m3 (fund record lines.volume), so the text now presents both years through volume placeholders rather than a typed path; the judge 4.58 reading does not reproduce from the current model [S10][S4].

challenges.challenge: Free float 7.7% and insider 92.3% are still cited to [S0] in section 1, and S0 is a Yahoo statements source with no archived text; the same paragraph already cites [S4] for the controller, so the figure has a proper home. This number anchors the zero-liquidity-discount decision, so an uncitable citation is not cosmetic. QC Q2 is unresponded.
challenges.answer: Adopted the Q2 fix in full: float and insider figures are cited to the annual report shareholding table at [S4], the duplicate S0 citation in sections 5-6 is gone, and the deck-marker sentences no longer lean on S0 for content it does not carry. The zero-liquidity-discount decision therefore rests on a citable shareholding table plus the traded-value data [S4].

missing_bull_case.note: Base and bull both cap volume at 4.75m m3 (85% of 5.58m) and assume no new plant, so a sixth line is worth zero although BLES built five plants in five years and management says it will add capacity when utilisation nears optimum [S10]. Payout is frozen at 20%, so net cash reaches Rp2.57tn (Rp289/sh) by FY2035 earning 3%. Terminal 3.5% nominal is ~0% real against the report's own multi-year substitution runway.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear (price -8%, volume -7%, GM -3pp) is milder than the last actual trough: FY2025 realised price was Rp411k (-15% vs 2026) on a 25.9% gross margin (-14pp), so the scenario never tests a repeat of 2025 and still prints Rp279 (+38%). No float/index-forced-placement, receivables or KDMP-payment stress, and the adjacent cement price war is not translated into a block price path.

assumption_realism.note: Documented price path (1% nominal, lt Rp505,000) is not what the model runs: FY2031E is Rp517,625 and FY2035E Rp571,361 (+2.5%/yr), 13% above the stated lt. FY2026 revenue of Rp1,940bn implies Q4 of Rp533bn vs a 9M average of Rp469bn while the text says Q4 runs at the Q3 rate. FY2026 gross margin of 42.0% at base cost exceeds the verified 9M actual of 40.3%.

evidence_and_citations.note: Verified in the archives: D&A Rp137.3bn with its COGS/selling/G&A split (S3); 9M revenue Rp1,407.3bn and gross profit Rp567.4bn (S2); volume 2.90273m m3, 69% utilisation, Rp284bn profit (S6); capex Rp261.5bn and 5.58m m3 capacity (S10, S4); 122/66Mt cement surplus (S11). Failures: no Rp70bn 2026 capex plan anywhere in S10; OCF did not cover capex (CFO Rp236.3bn vs capex Rp261.5bn); the 20% policy is one year's payout in S5; S8's 20% target was for 2024 not thereafter; free float prints as 771.0%.

valuation_method_fit.note: Through-cycle DCF at 80% is the right method for this cyclical, the 42.7% TV share is modest, and the Rp255.5bn bridge net debt reconciles to the Q3 balance sheet with only 25.2% of FY2026 prorated (no double count) — credit. But COE is computed as rf + beta*(ERP+CRP) - 0.0162 default_spread, so a debt spread is subtracted from equity: COE is 13.19% instead of the 14.81% the disclosed inputs imply and WACC should be ~13.2%, not 11.9%.

bias_and_tone.note: The report says the market price 'implies roughly the bear case', but the bear case is Rp279, 38% above the Rp202 price, and the extreme_call justification's reverse-DCF claim is asserted, not shown. 'The asymmetry is why we are buyers' rests on a bear that cannot lose money: doubling the bear probability to 50% with base 40/bull 10 still gives ~Rp346 (+71%). A 98% call needs a reverse-DCF table, not a sentence.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The engine reads the coal deck's ici4 (spot 65.06 vs FY2027E 52.5, contango) through the autoclave link, but the report never states the marker, the base-year price or the margin contribution, so 42% 'at base input costs' cannot be checked against the verified 40.3% actual. BLES is AAC, not cement; the 7.09x EV/EBITDA and 0.33x P/B medians come from cement peers (INTP, SMGR, SMBR, WTON, CMNT) and should be labelled as adjacent-industry cross-checks.

conservatism_audit.note: Below evidence or below guidance: capex 6.0% of sales (Rp116bn) against a claimed but unsourced Rp70bn plan; opex 13.5% vs 13.1% actual; terminal growth 3.5% nominal, below CPI alone (3.28%), implying negative real growth forever; payout 20% vs 44% trailing; volume capped at 85% utilisation with no expansion option. Shocks are mirrored in inputs (0.93/1.07 volume, 0.92/1.08 price, plus/minus 3pp GM) — credit — but the bear price step is smaller than the 2025 actual cut and the liquidity discount is 0.0%.

calibration.note: All four BLOCKs carry justifications whose sources say what is claimed, and the +16.9pp FY2026 margin step is an actual: 9M2026 EBITDA of Rp511bn (EBIT Rp383.3bn plus D&A Rp127.7bn) on Rp1,407bn is 36.3%, verified in S2, and FY2026E 35.0% is slightly below it. The weights.changed WARN (80/12/8 vs 60/25/15) is explained in section 4. The Q4 revenue build and the 42% GM are challenged under assumption_realism.

signoff.notes: APPROVED. BUY is defensible and the report states what its model does. BLES is not a commodity cement producer but the largest AAC block maker in Indonesia, so the CMNT parallel does not carry: CMNT is SELL at 13.7x FY2025 EV/EBITDA on a levered, loss-making book, while BLES trades at 2.7x FY2025 EV/EBITDA and 1.2x book. The 7.09x is the peer median applied to FY2025 trough EBITDA as a 12%-weight cross-check, which is why it prints Rp188 and P/BV Rp51; section 4 says this explicitly and does not average them up, and the bear, a full FY2025 repeat at Rp171, sits below the Rp194 price, so the price is bracketed between trough and base rather than by an unsourced uplift. Base is actual-led and slightly conservative: FY2026E EBITDA Rp656.7bn is 4% below the 9M2026 run-rate, revenue is the 9M annualised, the +16.9pp calibration step is measured from the FY2025 trough, and the 80/12/8 weights follow the commodity-cyclical card. Batch: CEMENT is not uniformly one-sided (CMNT SELL; three peers parked) and the 11.9% WACC is the sector build. Conditions to clear before the next version, QC FIX items that do not move the Rp413 target but are known false statements in a published document: Q1 the NWC basis says payables Rp168bn exceed receivables plus inventory Rp204bn when they are Rp36.5bn lower; Q2 beta 0.90 is a house industry default, not a peer-regression median; Q3 weight_basis claims P/BV excludes the Rp101.7bn revaluation reserve when the metric includes it (0.07% of target); Q4 407 employees vs the AR 358; Q5 1.5% of revenue is the FY2026 model assumption, not the 9M2026 actual (0.53%, 0.90% including advances); section 3 should read 42.0% FY2026 gross margin, not 39.7%, to match the model input; and section 5 should name the 15% minimum-float obligation and its 2029 date alongside the dilution risk. The prior return L1 and L2 material items are fixed and all facts and lint pass.

bias.note: Base is anchored to the last actual, not to a cautious haircut: FY2026E revenue Rp1,877.0bn is exactly 9M2026 Rp1,407.3bn annualised (3.87m m3 x Rp485k), and FY2026E EBITDA Rp656.7bn sits 4% BELOW the 9M2026 run-rate of Rp511bn x 4/3 = Rp681bn. Against that, the gross margin fades 42.0% (base input cost) to 33.0% by FY2035, only ~1pt above the FY2023-24 norm of 31-32%, opex is held at 13.5% vs 13.1% actual, price is flat in real terms from the 9M2026 level, volume rises only to 84% utilisation, and terminal growth 3.5% = deck inflation + 1pt, below nominal GDP. The bear is a sourced FY2025 repeat at Rp171 and the bull is capped by physical capacity at Rp623; the lopsided shocks are the margin arithmetic of each price path, not a bias. No unsourced optimism or conservatism moves the rating [S2][S3][S4][S6][S10][S11].

findings.finding: The nwc_pct basis says FY2025 payables of Rp168bn 'exceed' receivables plus inventory of Rp204bn; they are Rp36.5bn lower (trade payables Rp167.5bn vs receivables Rp137.7bn + inventory Rp66.4bn, S3 p.9). The -4% NWC input can be defended only on total operating liabilities (other payables Rp63.5bn + accruals Rp19.3bn + tax Rp14.5bn + contract liabilities Rp10.3bn), which the note never mentions. Valuation impact of the wording is nil; the stated arithmetic is false.

Section 4 says the beta is 'the industry unlevered median of 0.90'. The engine records beta_source as 'industry default (config)' and operating configuration sets beta_unlevered_default: 0.9 for CEMENT - it is a house sector default, not a computed peer-regression median. The 13.2% COE uses the same 0.90, so no number changes, but the evidence basis for the discount rate is overstated.

assumptions valuation.weight_basis claims P/BV is computed on 'equity excluding the Rp101.7bn PSAK 16 revaluation reserve [S3]'. The engine's pbv metric is Rp1,387.7bn, the total equity attributable to owners at 30 Sep 2026, which INCLUDES the Rp101,675,026,115 revaluation reserve (S2 p.5). Excluding it the P/BV value is Rp47.3, not Rp51.1 (0.3/share, 0.07% of target) - immaterial, but the method statement is false and contradicts section 3/6's instruction to use pre-revaluation equity.

Section 1 states the company 'has 407 employees [S4]'. The annual report says 358 employees at 2025 (246 male + 112 female), down from 440 in 2024 (S4 p.71). No source supports 407. Immaterial to the thesis but it is a fact cited to a source that does not contain it.

The capex_pct basis and the extreme_call justification call '1.5% of revenue' the 9M2026 actual. 9M2026 fixed-asset acquisitions were Rp7.49bn, 0.53% of Rp1,407bn revenue (0.90% including the Rp5.18bn of fixed-asset advances) [S2]. 1.5% is the rounded FY2026 model assumption (Rp28.2bn on Rp1,877bn), i.e. above the actual - conservative, not wrong in the model, but mislabelled as the actual.

Sections 3 and 4 print the block price as '485,000.0 IDR/t per cubic metre'. The CEMENT template unit is IDR/t but BLES prices AAC blocks per m3; the model input is IDR/m3. Unit label only - the number is right.

The second sensitivity grid (12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin) is flat across all five gross-margin columns - every row repeats one value - so a 1pp margin shock has no effect on the target while the scenario runs clearly re-price margin. If the grid is shown, it should be re-run on the margin axis.

The DCF bridge uses net debt Rp255.5bn at 30 Sep 2026, which nets Rp188.2bn cash plus Rp67.4bn of current 'other investments' [S2], and the DCF counts only Q4 FY2026 cash flow; the model's FY2026E closing net debt is Rp54.2bn. The DCF arithmetic ties, but section 4 never states the bridge date or that other investments are treated as cash, so a reader cannot reconcile 450 with the 54.2 in the financial table.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +16.9pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2025 was the trough, not the norm: the 9M2026 LK shows gross margin 40.3% and EBITDA Rp511bn (36.3% of Rp1,407bn sales) after the 2025 price cuts were reversed, so the +17pp step is an actual, not a forecast [S2][S6].

flags.message: a.volume moves +23% from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Volume rises 21% over seven years only as utilisation moves from 69% (9M2026) to 84% of the 5.58m m3 installed capacity; S10 says management judges the current five plants adequate and sees no short-term need for additions, while also flagging gradual expansion once utilisation nears optimal. No site, budget or timeline for an addition is disclosed, so the base underwrites the installed base only and treats expansion as upside [S4][S6][S10].

flags.message: a.gross_margin moves -9.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The 9pp fade by FY2035 returns the margin to the FY2023-24 31-32% level plus an efficiency gain, because FY2025 showed ASP can be cut to defend share and the adjacent cement market runs 45-46% overcapacity [S3][S4][S11][S13].

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves +6.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: FY2026 capex is set from the company's own 9M2026 cash-flow statement - Rp7.49bn of fixed-asset acquisitions plus Rp5.18bn of advances against Rp182.99bn in 9M2025 when Banjarnegara was completed - then lifted to 7.5% of revenue, the restated D&A share, as the asset base is renewed. There is no announced site, budget or timeline for a further plant, and the base credits neither new-plant volume nor new-plant capex, so the two sides are symmetric [S2][S3][S10].

flags.message: a.gross_margin: bear -0.1 vs bull 0.04 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: Gross margin is a ratio, so the same price move is not symmetric in margin points: FY2025 cut ASP to Rp411k/m3 and gross margin fell from 42% to 25.9%, while an 8% price rise on a 42% margin with flat unit cost adds only about 4pp; the bear's -10pp and the bull's +4pp are the margin arithmetic of each price path, not a bias [S3][S4].

flags.message: a.price: bear 0.847 vs bull 1.08 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: Bear price is the verified FY2025 realised price of about Rp411k/m3 against the FY2026 Rp485k/m3 (a 0.847 factor) [S3][S4][S2]; the bull's 1.08 is the 2026 recovery extending a further 8%, which is the only price move we can defend with evidence and is smaller because the 2025 cut was a share defence, not a normal trading range [S4].

flags.message: a.volume: bear 0.95 vs bull 1.116 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: Bull volume is capped at about 95% utilisation of the 5.58m m3 installed base, the practical maximum without an announced capacity addition [S4][S10], which is a 1.116 factor on base; the bear's 0.95 is the demand shortfall with capacity unchanged, so the two are bounded by physical capacity rather than mirror images [S4].

flags.message: expected return +117%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return to target rests on three sourced items: ASP restored to Rp485k/m3 from Rp411k [S2][S6], opex held at 13% of sales versus 17% in FY2025 [S2][S3], and capex at the 9M2026 actual of 1.5% of revenue with no announced new-plant programme [S2][S10]. Our bear case is the FY2025 trough repeat and it lands below the price, so the price sits between the bear and base scenarios; we call the size of the implied gap out in section 4 as the extreme reading rather than treating it as a forecast.
